notes.meaning: Hoshea seized the throne of Israel by murdering the previous king, but it took years of turmoil before his rule was firmly established. He governed in Samaria for nine years as the nineteenth and final king of the northern kingdom. His reign marked the closing chapter of a nation that had long walked away from God.

Hoshea did evil in God's eyes, yet he was not quite as wicked as the kings before him. He did not introduce new idols and even allowed his subjects to travel south to worship at the temple in Jerusalem. Even so, the sins of the nation had reached their limit, and judgment could no longer be delayed.

King Shalmaneser of Assyria marched his powerful army against Israel and forced Hoshea to surrender. Hoshea became his servant and had to pay heavy tribute, which was a yearly tax paid to keep peace. When God's people turn from Him, they often end up under the control of harsh worldly masters.

Hoshea stopped paying his yearly taxes to Assyria and secretly asked the king of Egypt to help him break free. Shalmaneser uncovered the plot, seized Hoshea, and threw him into prison. Looking to foreign nations instead of crying out to the Lord only sped up Israel's downfall.

The Assyrian army swept across the land of Israel and surrounded its capital city, Samaria. The siege lasted for three difficult years while the trapped people ran out of food and hope. Even the strongest city walls cannot protect people once God removes His shield over them.

Samaria finally fell, and the king of Assyria forced the people of Israel out of their homeland. The captives were scattered to distant places like Halah, the banks of the Habor River, and cities in Media. This marked the tragic end of the northern kingdom of Israel as an independent nation.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Ancient Assyrian royal inscriptions indicate that Sargon the Second finished capturing Samaria and deported its people after Shalmaneser died during the three-year siege.

notes.meaning: The writer pauses the story to explain why this disaster fell upon the nation. Israel had sinned against the Lord their God, the very One who had rescued them from slavery under Pharaoh in Egypt. Instead of loving and thanking their Deliverer, they feared and bowed down to other gods.

The Israelites adopted the wicked customs of the Canaanite nations that God had driven out before them. They also followed the false religious rules set up by their own kings, such as worshiping golden calves. By copying the evil habits of the people God had judged, they invited that same judgment on themselves.

The people tried to practice wrong things in secret against God, foolishly acting as if He could not see them. They built pagan shrines called high places everywhere, from solitary watchtowers in the fields to large walled cities. Idolatry was no longer an isolated sin; it had spread across every corner of the country.

The people set up sacred stone pillars to honor the false god Baal and wooden poles dedicated to the goddess Asherah. They placed these idols on top of high hills and under spreading shade trees where pagan worship was common. They filled the land God had given them with objects that broke His plain law.

Israel burned incense on all the pagan high places, copying the very nations God had destroyed and driven out. Burning incense was supposed to be a sacred act of worship and prayer reserved for the true God alone. Their stubborn defiance provoked the Lord to righteous anger.

The people gave their devotion to lifeless idols, even though the Lord had strictly commanded them never to make or worship images. These manufactured gods were worthless and dirty, having no power to help anyone. Turning to created things instead of the Creator always leads to ruin.

God did not judge His people without warning them first. He sent a steady stream of prophets and seers—messengers who received visions from God—urging both Israel and Judah to turn from their evil ways and obey His commandments. God showed remarkable patience by giving them countless chances to repent.

The people refused to listen and stiffened their necks in stubborn rebellion against God's call. Like an ox that fights against the wooden yoke across its neck, they would not submit to God's guidance. Their disobedience came from unbelief, because they did not really trust the Lord their God.

They cast aside God's rules and broke the covenant—the sacred promise—He had made with their ancestors. They chased after worthless, empty idols and ended up becoming spiritually empty and worthless themselves. People always become like the things they choose to worship.

The people tossed away all the commandments of the Lord and cast two metal calves to worship, repeating a famous sin from their past. They set up poles to honor the goddess Asherah, worshiped the sun, moon, and stars, and served the pagan god Baal. Their unfaithfulness was complete and touched every part of their lives.

They reached the lowest point of cruelty by sacrificing their own sons and daughters in fire to false gods. They sought guidance from fortune-tellers and evil spirits instead of listening to God's word. By selling themselves to do evil, they acted like willing slaves to sin and provoked the Lord's anger.

The Lord became very angry with Israel and removed the northern kingdom from His presence and special care. He cast them out of the Promised Land, leaving only the southern kingdom of Judah behind. Those who persistently push God away will eventually lose the blessing of His fellowship.

Even the southern tribe of Judah failed to obey the commandments of the Lord their God. Instead of learning a lesson from Israel's mistakes, Judah copied the corrupt religious practices that the northern kingdom had invented. Having the temple and God's law brought no protection to people who still chose to disobey.

The Lord rejected all the descendants of Israel, allowing raiders to afflict and plunder them until He finally drove them into exile. His earlier punishments were warnings meant to draw the people back, but their refusal to change made final judgment unavoidable. God is faithful to His word, both when He promises blessing and when He warns of judgment.
